guide.title: Astoria, Queens: Astor's Name, a WPA Pool and the Studio at 35-11 35th Avenue
guide.intro: Astoria is a Queens neighborhood named, along with Astoria Park and the pool inside it, for the fur merchant John Jacob Astor. NYC Parks records that Stephen Halsey, who founded the village of Astoria in 1839, named the area for his friend Astor, who lived from 1763 to 1848, and that the pool, the park and the surrounding neighborhood are all named after him. A Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report adds that Astor made a donation to build St. George's Episcopal Church. Astoria Park covers 59.96 acres and is carried by NYC Parks as a Community Park under ZIP codes 11102 and 11105. Also in the neighborhood are the Astoria Park Pool and Play Center, designated a landmark on June 20, 2006; the Famous Players-Lasky studio at 35-11 35th Avenue; Kaufman Astoria Studios at 34-12 36th Street; and the Museum of the Moving Image at 36-01 35th Avenue.

sections.heading: Astor's name, the park and the pool
sections.body:
NYC Parks' history of Astoria Park states that "Stephen Halsey, who founded the village of Astoria in 1839, named the area for his friend, fur merchant John Jacob Astor (1763-1848)," and that "the pool, park, and surrounding neighborhood are named after John Jacob Astor." A Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report puts the naming in commercial terms: Halsey and his associates "purportedly named the area Astoria to attract financial backing from millionaire John Jacob Astor, who made a donation to build St. George's Episcopal Church." The same NYC Parks history describes a Lenape village at Pot Cove.

The City files Astoria Park as a neighborhood tabulation area of its own, named Astoria Park. NYC Parks records it as a Community Park of 59.96 acres, Park ID Q004, Community Board 1, under ZIP codes 11102 and 11105. NYC Parks also records that "In 1926 community members gathered to dedicate the Astoria Park Memorial in tribute to the sons of Long Island City who died in World War I" — the municipal name the war dead's home city carried at the time.

The Astoria Park Pool and Play Center is addressed to 19th Street between 22nd Drive and Hoyt Avenue North and was designated a New York City landmark on June 20, 2006. Designation report LP-2196 says that "the Astoria Play Center commands a striking waterfront location in Astoria Park," and dates the opening of the pool complex to 1936. Writing about Robert Moses's siting of the eleven WPA pools of that year, the same report states: "Moses was also known to have been insensitive to people of color, and tried to restrict access to many of his recreational facilities, including the pools. He determined that the Colonial Park pool in Harlem would be the only one for minority use. Most of the other pools, including Astoria, were placed in white neighborhoods."

Athens Square, Park ID Q436, ZIP 11102, is described by NYC Parks as "a little bit of Athens in Astoria" and its text speaks of "Astoria's citizens." Of Hallets Cove Playground, ZIP 11102, NYC Parks writes that "Hallets Point was initially the commercial center of Astoria." Park signage installed in the late 1990s at Socrates Sculpture Park, on Vernon Boulevard in Long Island City, explains that name as chosen "both in honor of Socrates (469-399 B.C.), the great Greek philosopher, and also as a tribute to the people of Astoria, New York's largest Greek community."

sections.heading: Studios, a piano factory and burying grounds
sections.body:
Designation report LP-0977 heads its subject "PARAMOUNT STUDIOS, BUILDING NO.1 (MAIN BUILDING), 35-11 35th Avenue, Astoria, Borough of Queens," and its body places the Famous Players-Lasky studio "at 35-11 35th Avenue in Astoria, Queens." The City's neighborhood tabulation area for that address is named Astoria (Central). Kaufman Astoria Studios publishes its own address as 34-12 36th Street: one complex with two frontages, each carrying its own street number. The Museum of the Moving Image is at 36-01 35th Avenue, ZIP 11106.

On the river side of the neighborhood, the Sohmer & Company Piano Factory stands at 31-01 Vernon Boulevard, also given as 11-02 to 11-16 31st Avenue. Designation report LP-2172 calls it "one of the most prominent structures along the Queens side of the East River in Long Island City" and locates it "in the northern part of Long Island City near Astoria" — the report's own hedge, under a section headed "The Industrial Development of Long Island City/Astoria." The City's neighborhood tabulation area for the address is named Old Astoria-Hallets Point, and Epic Theatre Center, Inc. carries the same address, 31-01 Vernon Blvd, ZIP 11106.

The Lawrence Family Graveyard, at the southeast corner of 20th Road and 35th Street, dates to 1703; its 1966 designation report labels the address line "Steinway, Borough of Queens," while the body of the same report names "Miss Ruth Lawrence, the last member of the Lawrence family to live in Astoria." The Moore-Jackson Cemetery is recorded at 51st to 54th Streets between 31st and 32nd Avenues.

The Greater Astoria Historical Society, at 32-63 48 Street, ZIP 11103, has served the Borough of Queens since 1985. Bohemian Hall & Beer Garden publishes its address as 29-19 24th Avenue, Astoria, NY 11102. Taverna Kyclades, at 36-01 Ditmars Blvd, ZIP 11105, describes itself on its own site as Greek and "in Astoria Queens." Sweet Afton is at 30-09 34th St, and its own site calls it "Astoria's Neighborhood spot." Bahari Estiatorio is at 31-14 Broadway.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The subway line named for Astoria carries nine stations: seven in Queens, Queensboro Plaza among them, and two in Manhattan. The neighborhood's own stations include Astoria–Ditmars Blvd and Steinway Street.

Astoria Park is carried by NYC Parks under ZIP codes 11102 and 11105 and Park ID Q004. The pool inside it has its own address line: 19th Street between 22nd Drive and Hoyt Avenue North. Athens Square is recorded under ZIP 11102 and Park ID Q436, and Hallets Cove Playground under ZIP 11102.

The neighborhood's landmarks and institutions are reached by street number. The Famous Players-Lasky studio is at 35-11 35th Avenue and the Museum of the Moving Image at 36-01 35th Avenue, with Kaufman Astoria Studios at 34-12 36th Street. On the water, the Sohmer & Company Piano Factory is at 31-01 Vernon Boulevard, also given as 11-02 to 11-16 31st Avenue. The Lawrence Family Graveyard is at the southeast corner of 20th Road and 35th Street; the Moore-Jackson Cemetery runs from 51st to 54th Streets between 31st and 32nd Avenues.

faq.answer: The subway line named for Astoria carries nine stations: seven in Queens, Queensboro Plaza among them, and two in Manhattan. The neighborhood's own stations include Astoria–Ditmars Blvd and Steinway Street. Astoria Park is carried by NYC Parks under ZIP codes 11102 and 11105 and Park ID Q004, and the pool inside it under 19th Street between 22nd Drive and Hoyt Avenue North. faq.question: Why is it called Astoria?
faq.answer: For the fur merchant John Jacob Astor, who lived from 1763 to 1848. NYC Parks records that "Stephen Halsey, who founded the village of Astoria in 1839, named the area for his friend, fur merchant John Jacob Astor," and that "the pool, park, and surrounding neighborhood are named after John Jacob Astor." A Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report gives the motive as financial, saying the founders "purportedly named the area Astoria to attract financial backing from millionaire John Jacob Astor, who made a donation to build St. George's Episcopal Church."

faq.question: What is the Astoria Park Pool and Play Center?
faq.answer: A New York City landmark at 19th Street between 22nd Drive and Hoyt Avenue North, inside Astoria Park, designated on June 20, 2006. Designation report LP-2196 says "the Astoria Play Center commands a striking waterfront location in Astoria Park" and dates the opening of the pool complex to 1936. Writing about Robert Moses and the eleven WPA pools of that year, the report states: "Moses was also known to have been insensitive to people of color, and tried to restrict access to many of his recreational facilities, including the pools. He determined that the Colonial Park pool in Harlem would be the only one for minority use. Most of the other pools, including Astoria, were placed in white neighborhoods."

faq.question: Which film studios are in Astoria?
faq.answer: Designation report LP-0977 heads its subject "PARAMOUNT STUDIOS, BUILDING NO.1 (MAIN BUILDING), 35-11 35th Avenue, Astoria, Borough of Queens," and its body puts the Famous Players-Lasky studio "at 35-11 35th Avenue in Astoria, Queens." Kaufman Astoria Studios publishes its address as 34-12 36th Street — the same complex, a second frontage, a second street number. The Museum of the Moving Image is at 36-01 35th Avenue, ZIP 11106.

faq.question: Where are Astoria's old burying grounds?
faq.answer: The Lawrence Family Graveyard is at the southeast corner of 20th Road and 35th Street and dates to 1703. Its 1966 designation report labels the address line "Steinway, Borough of Queens," while the body of the same report names "Miss Ruth Lawrence, the last member of the Lawrence family to live in Astoria." The Moore-Jackson Cemetery is recorded at 51st to 54th Streets between 31st and 32nd Avenues.

photos.title: Hell Gate Bridge from Astoria Park
photos.description: A paved path curves through Astoria Park past a lit lamppost and a bench, with bare autumn trees and fallen leaves over the grass. The steel arch of the Hell Gate Bridge carries its rail deck overhead, and beyond it the towers and cables of a suspension bridge stand against a yellow sunset on the East River, where a few people walk the waterfront railing.
photos.author: Kenneth C. Zirkel

photos.title: Astoria Park Pool and Play Center
photos.description: The filled outdoor pool holds pale green water inside a wide concrete deck edged in yellow, with a metal ladder rail at the near corner. A long brick bathhouse closes the far side, a clock set above its central entrance canopy, banked concrete seating tiers in front of it and flags flying from the railing along its roofline. Parks vehicles are parked on the deck under an overcast sky.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Famous Players-Lasky Studio (Paramount Studios, Building No. 1)
places.summary: A designated New York City landmark at 35-11 35th Avenue. Designation report LP-0977 heads it "PARAMOUNT STUDIOS, BUILDING NO.1 (MAIN BUILDING), 35-11 35th Avenue, Astoria, Borough of Queens," and its body places the building "at 35-11 35th Avenue in Astoria, Queens."
places.history: The City's neighborhood tabulation area for the address is named Astoria (Central). The building shares its complex with Kaufman Astoria Studios, which publishes a separate street number, 34-12 36th Street.

photos.title: Paramount Studios, Building No. 1, at 35th Avenue and 35th Street
photos.description: The grey corner facade of the landmark studio building, its tall multi-pane windows set between shallow pilasters and dark banners reading Kaufman Astoria Studios hung at the roofline. A covered entrance porch on square piers runs along the 35th Avenue front under a flag on a pole, and pedestrians cross the sunlit sidewalk at the corner beneath a partly cloudy sky.
photos.author: Jim.henderson
